name: Habsburg
summary: From a Swabian comital lineage to the house that brought together the Empire, Austria, Bohemia, Hungary, the Spanish Monarchy and the Low Countries, before dividing into Austrian and Spanish branches in 1556.
origin: The Habsburgs take their name from Habsburg Castle in what is now the Swiss canton of Aargau. Rudolf I, elected King of the Romans in 1273, defeated Ottokar II of Bohemia and granted Austria and Styria to his sons in 1282, establishing the family’s territorial base for centuries. Albert I also became King of the Romans. From the fifteenth century onward, the family held the imperial dignity almost continuously.
history: After Albert II was elected King of the Romans in 1438 and Frederick III in 1440, royal and then imperial authority remained almost continuously in the house. Frederick’s son Maximilian married Mary of Burgundy in 1477. The marriage of Philip the Handsome to Joanna of Castile, and the marriages of Maximilian’s grandchildren to the Jagiellons, enabled Charles V and Ferdinand I to bring together Castile, Aragon, Italian territories, the Low Countries, Austria, Bohemia and Hungary. During Charles V’s abdications of 1555–1556, Philip II received the Spanish Monarchy while Ferdinand I retained the Central European lands and was recognised as emperor in 1558.
legacy: The Spanish branch ended with Charles II in 1700, and the dispute over his inheritance triggered the War of the Spanish Succession. The Austrian male line ended with Charles VI in 1740; his daughter Maria Theresa, married to Francis Stephen of Lorraine, founded the House of Habsburg-Lorraine. Frequent marriages within both branches help explain several of their succession crises.

name: Bjälbo
summary: Birger Jarl’s family linked the Swedish monarchy with Norway and, through its daughters and marriages, with Mecklenburg and Denmark.
origin: The sons of Birger Jarl brought the House of Bjälbo to the Swedish throne. Some scholarship calls the dynasty Folkung, a name also applied to political groups in medieval Sweden.
history: Conflict among the sons of Magnus III led to King Birger’s fall. Magnus, the son of Erik Magnusson and Ingeborg of Norway, inherited Norway and was elected king in Sweden. His sister Euphemia connected the family with Mecklenburg, and his son Haakon VI married Margaret of Denmark.
legacy: Olaf, the son of Haakon and Margaret, died without issue. The continuity of the unions passed to other houses related to Bjälbo through elections, inheritance and marriage alliances.

name: Nasrid
summary: The Banū Naṣr ruled the Kingdom of Granada and created an exceptionally rich palatial capital at the Alhambra.
origin: Muhammad ibn Nasr, known as Ibn al-Ahmar, was proclaimed at Arjona in 1232 and entered Granada in 1238. The Pact of Jaén with Ferdinand III in 1246 consolidated the emirate under obligations of vassalage and tribute to Castile.
history: The emirs alternated between alliances and wars with Castile, Aragon and the Marinids of North Africa. The succession passed through different family branches. Fatima, daughter of Muhammad II, transmitted decisive rights to the throne to her son Ismail I. Yusuf I and Muhammad V sponsored major palatial works.
legacy: Internal disputes in the fifteenth century weakened political continuity. Abu al-Hasan Ali, Boabdil and al-Zagal led rival causes during the war against the Catholic Monarchs. Granada’s surrender in January 1492 ended Nasrid sovereignty. The Alhambra, its inscriptions and its archives preserve the dynasty’s memory.

name: Brabant
summary: The counts of Leuven built a duchy whose succession depended on family ties as well as on its towns and estates.
origin: The Leuven family acquired the ducal title of Lower Lotharingia in 1106. Henry I consolidated the Duchy of Brabant in the late twelfth century. Major urban centres, including Leuven and Brussels, provided resources to a dynasty situated between France and the Empire.
history: John I secured Limburg after the Battle of Worringen in 1288. John II granted the Charter of Kortenberg, and John III combined marriage alliances with the defence of the duchy. When he died in 1355, his daughter Joanna inherited it with her husband Wenceslaus of Luxembourg.
legacy: The Joyous Entry of 1356 recognised the rights and guarantees demanded by the Brabantine estates. The inheritance later passed to Anthony of Burgundy, grandson of Joanna’s sister. The change of dynasty preserved the importance of these institutions and linked Brabant with the wider territories of the Burgundian dukes.

name: Castiglione-Mantua
summary: The Mantuan family of the humanist Baldassare Castiglione, author of The Book of the Courtier, was linked to the Gonzaga and Torelli houses.
origin: Cristoforo Castiglione and Luigia, or Aloisa, Gonzaga were Baldassare’s parents. The family held estates around Mantua and maintained ties with the city’s ruling house.
history: Baldassare was born at Casatico in 1478, served at Mantua and Urbino, and married Ippolita Torelli in 1516. His diplomatic career took him to Rome and Spain, where he served as Clement VII’s nuncio to Charles V.
legacy: The Book of the Courtier, published in 1528, turned the conversations of the Urbino court into a model of education and conduct. Baldassare’s writing and diplomatic career gave the family a reputation that reached Rome and the court of Charles V.

name: Borja
summary: A Valencian family reached the papacy and turned its Italian and Iberian alliances into an extensive network of power.
origin: The Borjas originated in the Kingdom of Valencia. Alfonso de Borja pursued an ecclesiastical and diplomatic career before his election as Pope Callixtus III in 1455. His nephew Rodrigo became a cardinal and held a central place in the Roman Curia for decades.
history: Rodrigo was elected Pope Alexander VI in 1492. His children participated in a policy of alliances with Italy’s ruling houses: Lucrezia eventually married Alfonso d’Este, while Cesare created a territorial dominion in Romagna. The Italian Wars and the pope’s death in 1503 destroyed much of that project.
legacy: The dukes of Gandía consolidated their inheritance in the Iberian Peninsula. Francis Borgia renounced ducal life, entered the Society of Jesus and became its third superior general. Offices and marriages extended the family’s presence and connected it with other houses of the Spanish nobility.

name: Frankopan
summary: A Croatian house connected with the Zrinskis through marriages spanning more than one generation.
origin: The Frankopans were a Croatian noble house with several branches. In the sixteenth century Katarina married Nikola IV Zrinski. In the next generation, Vuk Krsto fathered Ana Katarina and Fran Krsto, who were likewise connected with the Zrinskis.
history: Ana Katarina and Fran Krsto, Vuk’s children, shared political and cultural ties with Italy and the Zrinskis. She married Petar Zrinski; Fran Krsto became Petar’s brother-in-law and fellow conspirator. Writing and estate management formed part of the family’s activity.
legacy: Fran Krsto’s execution and Ana Katarina’s imprisonment followed the crisis of 1670. Their literary work and the descendants of Jelena Zrinski carry the family’s history beyond that outcome.

summary: The creation of Orléans for Gaston, Louis XIII’s brother, belongs to a different line from the one later founded by Philip I.
origin: Gaston, son of Henry IV and Marie de’ Medici and brother of Louis XIII, received the Duchy of Orléans in 1626. Philip I, his nephew and a son of Louis XIII, became the head of a new creation of the duchy in 1661.
history: Gaston’s daughters married into several European courts. Marguerite Louise, his daughter by Marguerite of Lorraine, married Cosimo III de’ Medici and became Grand Duchess of Tuscany.
legacy: Gaston’s male line ended with his death in 1660. His daughters retained their property rights and alliances. The arms of Orléans, with a silver label over the lilies of France, continued in Philip I’s new ducal creation.
